Rethinking American Holidays: The Case for Abolishing Columbus Day

Introduction

Every October, the United States pauses to observe Columbus Day—a federal holiday that, on its surface, celebrates the 1492 arrival of Christopher Columbus in the Americas. Yet beneath the veneer of discovery and adventure lies a legacy profoundly at odds with the values modern America claims to uphold: human dignity, justice, and equality. The continued observance of Columbus Day represents a troubling refusal to reckon honestly with history. It is time for the United States to abolish this holiday and, in doing so, take a meaningful step toward acknowledging the truth of its founding and honoring the peoples who were here long before any European ship touched these shores.

I. The Myth of Discovery

For generations, American schoolchildren learned a sanitized narrative: in 1492, a brave Italian explorer sailed the ocean blue and "discovered" a New World. This framing is not merely incomplete—it is fundamentally dishonest. The Americas were home to an estimated 50 to 100 million people at the time of Columbus's arrival. Complex civilizations flourished across the continents: the Aztec capital of Tenochtitlán was larger and more architecturally sophisticated than most European cities of the era; the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy had developed a democratic governance structure that would later inspire American founders; and the Maya had advanced systems of mathematics, astronomy, and writing.

To celebrate Columbus as a "discoverer" is to erase these civilizations from history, to declare that only European presence confers legitimacy on a land. It perpetuates the Doctrine of Discovery—the medieval European legal principle that authorized Christian nations to claim sovereignty over non-Christian lands—an ideology that has been used for centuries to justify dispossession and violence against Indigenous peoples. The word "discovery" itself carries an implicit judgment: that the people already living here were invisible, their humanity and achievements unworthy of recognition.

II. Columbus the Man: A Record of Cruelty

If the holiday merely rested on a historical inaccuracy, one might argue it is a harmless anachronism. But the case against Columbus goes far beyond semantic quibbles. The man himself was responsible for acts of extraordinary brutality.

When Columbus arrived in the Caribbean, he encountered the Taíno people—a population estimated at between 250,000 and several million across the islands of the Greater Antilles. His own journals and the accounts of those who traveled with him paint a damning picture. In a 1493 letter to the Spanish monarchs, Columbus noted that the Taíno were "fit to be ordered about and made to work," eagerly envisioning their enslavement. In a letter to Luis de Santángel, he wrote that the Taíno "would make fine servants" and that "with fifty men we could subjugate them all and make them do whatever we want."

As governor of Hispaniola, Columbus instituted a brutal tribute system requiring every Taíno adult over the age of fourteen to deliver a specific quantity of gold every three months. Those who failed to meet their quota had their hands cut off. Those who resisted were subjected to systematic violence: mutilation, enslavement, and massacre. The Spanish conquistador Bartolomé de las Casas, who initially participated in the colonial project before becoming its most outspoken critic, documented these atrocities in his Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1552). He described soldiers testing the sharpness of their swords on Taíno prisoners, the enslavement of entire communities, and mass suicides by Indigenous people who preferred death to continued subjugation.

The result was demographic catastrophe. Within decades of Columbus's arrival, the Taíno population was reduced by an estimated 90 percent—through a combination of disease, enslavement, murder, and starvation caused by the destruction of their agricultural systems. While European diseases were a significant factor in this depopulation, it is historically dishonest to attribute the genocide solely to pathogens. Disease was accelerated and compounded by deliberate colonial policies: forced labor, displacement, destruction of food sources, and outright violence.

Columbus himself, far from being an unwitting vector of disease, actively pursued the enslavement and exploitation of Indigenous peoples. In 1495, he shipped approximately 500 Taíno captives to Spain to be sold at auction. When the Spanish crown expressed discomfort with this practice, Columbus proposed establishing slave markets in the colonies. His governance was so brutal and so incompetent that the Spanish Crown eventually stripped him of his titles and had him arrested in 1500—though he was later pardoned and permitted to make a fourth voyage.

III. A Holiday That Honors Colonialism

Supporters of Columbus Day often argue that the holiday celebrates Italian-American heritage rather than the man himself, and that it marks the beginning of European civilization in the Americas. Both arguments deserve serious scrutiny.

The first claim—that Columbus Day is about Italian pride—deserves empathy but ultimately fails as a justification. Italian Americans, many of whom faced discrimination in the 19th and early 20th centuries, embraced Columbus as a symbol of their contributions to American history. This is understandable, and the desire for cultural recognition is legitimate. But cultural pride need not be tethered to a figure whose legacy is inseparable from genocide. Italian American identity is extraordinarily rich—encompassing contributions to art, science, philosophy, music, cuisine, governance, and social justice—that hardly requires the celebration of a 15th-century slaver as its standard-bearer. One can honor Italian American heritage without endorsing the worst chapters of colonial history.

The second claim—that the holiday marks the beginning of European civilization in the Americas—reveals the deeper problem. To frame colonization as a positive starting point is to take a decidedly European-centric view of American history. For Indigenous peoples, 1492 does not mark a beginning. It marks the beginning of an apocalypse. The centuries that followed brought the Trail of Tears, the Sand Creek Massacre, the forced assimilation of children in residential schools, the destruction of treaty after treaty, and systematic efforts to eradicate Indigenous languages, cultures, and legal systems. Celebrating Columbus Day implicitly endorses the narrative that European colonization was an unqualified good—that the benefits of Western civilization outweigh the costs of Indigenous destruction. This is a moral calculus that Indigenous peoples were never invited to participate in, and it is one that history has thoroughly discredited.

IV. The Harm of Historical Celebration

Some may argue that abolishing Columbus Day amounts to "erasing history" or capitulating to "political correctness." This objection inverts reality. Keeping Columbus Day on the federal calendar is itself an act of historical erasure—a selective memorialization that honors the colonizer while rendering the colonized invisible.

We do not need to forget Columbus to stop celebrating him. The United States maintains museums, archives, academic programs, and public monuments dedicated to the full, complex, often painful story of American history. What it should not do is elevate a man responsible for enslavement and mass death to a position of public honor. There is a meaningful distinction between studying history and venerating it. We teach our children about World War II without celebrating Adolf Hitler; we study the Roman Empire without declaring every Roman emperor a hero. Historical literacy requires honesty, not hagiography.

Moreover, the continued existence of Columbus Day sends a clear message to Indigenous communities—communities that still bear the intergenerational trauma of colonization—that their suffering is an acceptable price for someone else's celebration. Native Americans suffer disproportionately from poverty, health disparities, educational inequity, and suicide. The rates of missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls remain a national crisis. In this context, a federal holiday honoring the man who initiated the chain of events leading to these conditions is not merely tone-deaf. It is a form of ongoing institutional disrespect.

V. A Growing Consensus

The movement to abolish Columbus Day is not a fringe position. It reflects a growing national consensus. More than 200 cities across the United States have replaced Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day, including major metropolitan areas like Los Angeles, Chicago, Denver, Seattle, and New York City. States including Maine, Vermont, New Mexico, Oregon, and Alaska have made the change at the state level. Even the federal government has taken tentative steps: in 2021, President Biden became the first president to issue a proclamation recognizing Indigenous Peoples' Day.

This shift reflects not political extremism but moral maturation. It represents a society capable of updating its public symbols to reflect its deepest values. The abolition of Columbus Day does not require us to achieve perfection in our treatment of Indigenous peoples; it requires only that we stop actively honoring the person most responsible for their historical suffering.

VI. What Replacing Columbus Day Would Mean

Abolishing Columbus Day—and replacing it with Indigenous Peoples' Day or another commemorative observance—would serve multiple vital functions.

It would affirm the humanity of Indigenous peoples. For Native American communities, seeing the federal government formally acknowledge the harm of colonization would be a powerful, if symbolic, act of recognition. Symbols matter. They shape public consciousness, influence educational curricula, and signal what a society values.

It would promote historical literacy. A day dedicated to Indigenous history and contributions would encourage Americans to learn about the full scope of American history—not just the narrative of European expansion, but the stories of the peoples who shaped this land for millennia before Columbus's arrival.

It would align federal policy with American values. The United States professes commitment to human rights, dignity, and justice. A holiday that celebrates a figure associated with genocide and slavery fundamentally contradicts those commitments. Aligning our national calendar with our stated values is a basic exercise in institutional integrity.

Conclusion

The abolition of Columbus Day is not an act of erasure—it is an act of correction. It is a decision to tell the truth about history rather than perpetuate a myth that glorifies conquest and minimizes suffering. Christopher Columbus was not a hero whose achievements merit a national holiday. He was a man whose ambitions set in motion centuries of genocide, dispossession, and cultural destruction whose consequences reverberate to this day.

The United States has an opportunity—not to forget its past, but to confront it honestly. Replacing Columbus Day with a holiday that honors Indigenous peoples and their resilience would represent a small but profoundly meaningful act of justice. It would say, clearly and publicly, that American history belongs to all of its peoples, and that the lives and dignity of Indigenous communities are not footnotes to someone else's story of discovery.

It is time to close this chapter of willful mythmaking and begin writing a new one—grounded in truth, respect, and a genuine commitment to the values we claim to hold dear.

Title: A Day of Reckoning: Honoring Truth, Celebrating Resilience

Friends, neighbors, fellow citizens—

We gather today to speak of a holiday, but more than that, to speak of truth. To speak of whose stories we choose to honor, whose pain we choose to ignore, and what kind of legacy we, as a nation, wish to uphold.

For too long, on the second Monday of October, we have casually celebrated a man whose arrival set in motion a catastrophe—a catastrophe of disease, dispossession, and genocide against the Indigenous peoples of this hemisphere.

We have called it Columbus Day. A day of discovery.

But what was “discovered”? A land already home to millions. A land with complex societies, rich cultures, profound knowledge, and deep spiritual traditions. The only thing “discovered” was a new theater for old, brutal European ambitions: greed, domination, and conquest.

Christopher Columbus was not a heroic explorer. He was a merchant of human lives. In his own journals, he wrote of the Taíno people, “They ought to make good and skilled servants.” And so began the enslavement, the mutilations, the massacres. He instituted a tribute system so brutal that it drove countless people to suicide. He opened the door to the Columbian Exchange, which brought waves of disease that decimated populations by up to 90%.

To celebrate this man is to celebrate the beginning of an unbroken thread of injustice. It is to tell the descendants of those who survived the Smallpox blankets, the Trail of Tears, the boarding schools meant to “kill the Indian, save the man,” and the ongoing struggles for sovereignty and clean water: Your pain is not worthy of our national remembrance. Your conqueror’s statue deserves a pedestal.

This is not about erasing history. It is about ceasing to glorify a perpetrator. It is about finally, fully writing the victims back into the story.

Look at what we have instead of a celebration of a conqueror: the vibrant, enduring spirit of Indigenous nations. From the Haudenosaunee Confederacy’s influence on democratic ideals, to the agricultural genius that gave the world corn, potatoes, and chocolate. From profound ecological wisdom that we desperately need today, to a resilience that has preserved languages, ceremonies, and a sense of identity against unimaginable odds.

So today, we don’t just condemn Columbus. We call for his holiday’s elimination not to leave a void, but to fill it with something better.

We call for Indigenous Peoples’ Day.

A day of learning. A day where our children study the true history of this land. A day where we honor the treaties we have broken and listen to the voices of the original stewards of this earth. A day that recognizes that the story of America didn’t begin in 1492—it only took its most violent modern turn.

Let us replace a day of myth-making with a day of truth-telling. Let us replace a celebration of colonization with a celebration of survival and culture. Let us stand on the right side of history, finally.

This isn’t about taking something away. It’s about making something right. It’s about building a nation that is mature enough to face its own shadows, strong enough to apologize, and wise enough to honor all of its people.

Let this be our legacy: a nation that chooses respect over myth, justice over comfort, and life over a lie. Let us retire the myth of Columbus, and in his place, raise up the enduring, defiant, beautiful light of Indigenous history, present, and future.

Thank you.

Title: The Call to Abolish Columbus Day: Unveiling the Truth Behind the Legacy

The commemoration of Christopher Columbus on federal holidays stands testament to the pride the United States takes in its rich history. From a young age, we learn how Columbus' voyage of discovery paved the way for the exploration and establishment of America. His voyage is portrayed as a path-breaking endeavor, thus memorializing his name in history books with a grandeur often reserved for eminent pioneers. However, the known narrative of his exploit is not wholly accurate and fails to acknowledge the brutality that marked this historical epoch. Christopher Columbus's legacy, tainted with numerous accounts of colonialism, genocide, and exploitation of Indigenous peoples, needs to be scrutinized rather than celebrated. Thus, I implore the abolition of Columbus Day as a federal holiday.

The celebratory perspective supposedly honors an explorer, but inadvertently glorifies a colonizer. The glorification of Columbus bypasses the horrors inflicted upon the Native communities during his expeditions. Columbus' arrival in America marked the onset of destructive colonization: true, he opened up the New World for exploration, but at the expense of those originally inhabiting these lands. Impelled by greed for wealth and prominence, Columbus disregarded the natives' autonomy and commenced an era of coercive conversion, forced labor, and subjugation.

Disturbingly, Columbus's ambition led to an unprecedented genocide. Historians estimate that nearly three million Taíno people – who were the principal inhabitants of the Caribbean islands Columbus first landed – died as a result of his four voyages. Diseases like smallpox, afforded no resistance from the immune systems of the indigenous people, extinguished their populations. This tragedy shouldn't merely be regarded as an unintentional accident; it was the direct result of Columbus's reckless disregard for the well-being of indigenous populations, symptomatic of his broader, dehumanizing colonial conduct.

To add further insult and distress to indigenous heritage and history, Columbus was known to have established the first transatlantic slave trade. His disregard for indigenous rights set in motion centuries of systemic exploitation and devaluation of these peoples' cultures, contributions, and lives. However, our nation doesn't simply honor Columbus—it abets the erasure of these grim truths, effectively sanctioning the great injustices carried out by him.

To acknowledge Columbus Day is not merely a celebration of an explorer, but a validation of colonialism, genocide and exploitation. A national holiday is not supposed to be a day of mourning for entire communities. However, for the indigenous people, Columbus Day is a somber reminder of their historical sufferings, loss, and ongoing struggle against systemic injustices. Celebrating the holiday essentially rubs salt into the wounds of centuries-old atrocities enacted upon them.

Instead of Columbus Day, celebrating Indigenous Peoples’ Day would involve an acknowledgment of the rich history, heritage, and contribution of the original inhabitants of the American land. The commemoration would communicate the essential message of unity, respect, and value for all ethnic groups forming the diverse tapestry of America.

In summary, acknowledging Columbus Day as a federal holiday fosters enduring historical inaccuracies concerning the founding of the United States and undermines the immense suffering of the original inhabitants of the land we now call home. Abolition of Columbus Day doesn't attempt to hide our nation's past, but rather pushes to address it more honestly. As a country that stands firmly for truth, justice and equality, we ought to rethink our celebration of Columbus Day, shifting our focus to recognizing the rich heritage of our nation's indigenous ancestors instead.

In keeping with rights and respect, let us choose to celebrate Indigenous Peoples’ Day, honoring the true pioneers of the American landscape, rather than commemorating a figure that stands as a symbol of oppression for our indigenous population.

Introduction

His own journals and the accounts of his contemporaries reveal a man driven by greed, who immediately upon arrival in the Caribbean began to enslave, brutalize, and exterminate the Indigenous Taíno people.

Columbus wrote in his journal upon first contact: "They ought to make good and skilled servants, for they repeat very quickly whatever we say to them... with fifty men they could all be kept in subjection and forced to do whatever one wishes." This was not the observation of a curious explorer, but the assessment of a slave trader. Within decades of his arrival, the Taíno population, estimated between 250,000 and several million, was reduced by over 90% through a combination of enslavement, brutal working conditions in gold mines, mass executions, and the introduction of European diseases.

The systems of exploitation Columbus implemented—particularly the encomienda and repartimiento forced labor systems—became the blueprint for centuries of colonial oppression throughout the Americas. His governance of Hispaniola was so brutal that even contemporary Spanish officials, including Bartolomé de las Casas, condemned it as cruel and inhumane. De las Casas, who initially participated in the colonization, later documented horrific atrocities in his A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, describing systematic mutilation, torture, and genocide.

The establishment of Columbus Day as a federal holiday in 1937 was not primarily about celebrating historical discovery. It was championed by the Knights of Columbus and other groups during a period when Italian Americans faced significant discrimination. While the desire for cultural recognition is understandable, the choice of Columbus as a symbol was historically and morally problematic. It tied Italian American pride to a figure whose legacy is inseparable from the oppression of other marginalized groups.

This doctrine, rooted in 15th-century papal bulls, declared that non-Christian lands were available for European claim. Rethinking National Heroes: The Case for Abolishing Columbus Day

Introduction

Every second Monday of October, Americans observe Columbus Day — a federal holiday ostensibly commemorating Christopher Columbus's 1492 arrival in the Americas. For generations, schoolchildren learned a sanitized tale of a bold explorer who "discovered" a New World. Yet as our historical understanding has matured, a far more accurate and troubling portrait has emerged: Christopher Columbus was not a noble pioneer but the architect of colonialism, exploitation, and mass suffering on an unprecedented scale. It is time for the United States to formally abolish Columbus Day as a federal holiday — not to erase history, but to align our national commemorations with the values of justice, truth, and respect for human dignity.

I. The Historical Record: Columbus's Legacy of Violence

The argument against honoring Columbus does not rest on presentism or hasty judgment. It rests on what Columbus himself documented and what contemporary chroniclers recorded.

A. The Enslavement of Indigenous Peoples

Upon arriving in the Caribbean, Columbus immediately recognized the Taíno people's vulnerability and moved to exploit it. In a letter to the Spanish monarchs in 1493, he wrote admiringly of the islanders' willingness to serve, suggesting they would make excellent laborers. On Hispaniola, he established the encomienda system — a brutal framework of forced labor that amounted to chattel slavery. Taíno men, women, and children were compelled to mine gold, work plantations, and pay exorbitant tributes under penalty of mutilation or death.

Columbus himself overseen the shipping of hundreds of enslaved Taíno people back to Spain in 1495. When the Spanish Crown expressed reservations, Columbus proposed a different scheme: forced labor on the island with a tax of gold dust or cotton, cutting off the hands of those who failed to meet quotas. This is not the behavior of a misunderstood figure taken out of context — it is the deliberate policy of a colonial administrator who viewed Indigenous lives as instruments of profit.

B. Mass Death and Genocide

The arrival of Columbus set in motion a demographic catastrophe. While the introduction of European diseases played a significant role in population decline, the violence perpetrated by Columbus and his men was immediate and devastating.

On Hispaniola, the Taíno population is estimated to have been between 250,000 and several million at the time of contact. Within a few decades, it had been reduced to near extinction. Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish priest who witnessed these atrocities firsthand, documented in A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1552) the systematic murder, torture, and exploitation of Indigenous people by Columbus's subordinates — acts that Columbus authorized, encouraged, or willfully ignored.

Columbus's governorship was so brutal that even his Spanish contemporaries criticized him. He was eventually arrested and returned to Spain in chains in 1500, accused of tyranny and cruelty. This was not a retroactive moral judgment — it was a contemporaneous indictment.

C. The Doctrine of Discovery

Columbus's voyages gave birth to the Doctrine of Discovery — a legal and theological framework asserting that European "discoverers" had sovereign rights over non-Christian lands and peoples. This doctrine was enshrined in international law and later cited in U.S. Supreme Court decisions, including Johnson v. M'Intosh (1823), to justify the dispossession of Native American lands. The legacy of Columbus is therefore not merely historical; it is embedded in the legal structures that continue to affect Indigenous communities today.

II. Why a Federal Holiday Honors the Wrong Legacy

A. Federal Holidays Are Statements of National Values

A federal holiday is not a neutral observation. It is a deliberate act of national commemoration — a statement about who and what a society chooses to elevate. When the federal government declares Columbus Day, it signals approval and reverence for the figure it honors. By maintaining this holiday, the United States implicitly endorses a narrative that diminishes the suffering of millions of Indigenous people.

We do not celebrate every historical figure who played a role in shaping the nation. We select those whose legacies align with our aspirational values. Columbus's legacy — colonialism, enslavement, and the decimation of Indigenous populations — does not meet that threshold.

B. The Holiday Disregards Living Indigenous Communities

For the approximately 9.7 million people who identify as American Indian or Alaska Native in the United States, Columbus Day is not a celebration of heritage — it is a painful reminder of centuries of dispossession, cultural destruction, and ongoing systemic inequities. Indigenous communities have long called for the abolition of this holiday, and their voices must be centered in this conversation.

Since 1992, many cities and states have replaced Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day — a recognition that the narrative of "discovery" is inseparable from the narrative of destruction. Maintaining the federal holiday while localities opt out creates a dissonance in national identity: the federal government honors a figure whom communities across the country have explicitly rejected.

C. History Can Be Taught Without Celebration

Abolishing Columbus Day does not mean forgetting Christopher Columbus. It does not mean erasing history or whitewashing the past — indeed, the opposite is true. Removing the holiday forces a more honest and complete reckoning with the historical record. We can and should teach students about Columbus's voyages, the motivations behind them, and the catastrophic consequences that followed. But teaching is not the same as honoring. A federal holiday is an act of commemoration, not education.

III. Addressing Common Counterarguments

A. "Columbus Was a Man of His Time"

This argument attempts to shield Columbus behind the shield of historical relativism. But Columbus was not merely "a man of his time." He was criticized by his contemporaries. Spanish officials, clergy members, and even members of his own crew recognized and condemned his cruelty. The moral standards of the sixteenth century were not so low as to permit what Columbus did — indeed, the very existence of figures like Las Casas, who argued passionately for Indigenous rights, demonstrates that moral opposition to colonialism existed within Columbus's own world.

Moreover, if we accept the "man of his time" defense for Columbus, we must logically accept it for any historical figure, including those whose actions we universally condemn. The standard collapses into meaninglessness.

B. "Columbus Represents Italian-American Heritage"

Some defenders of Columbus Day argue that the holiday is important to Italian-Americans, for whom Columbus became a symbol of pride during an era of anti-Italian discrimination. This is a understandable and legitimate concern, but it does not require maintaining a federal holiday in Columbus's name. Italian-American contributions to the United States are vast and worthy of recognition — but they can be celebrated without honoring a figure whose legacy is inseparable from genocide. Furthermore, many Italian-Americans themselves have expressed support for renaming the holiday, recognizing that their heritage does not require the endorsement of colonialism.

C. "We Should Keep the Day as a Federal Holiday but Rename It"

This is a pragmatic compromise that has gained traction in many jurisdictions, and it has merit. Whether the day is simply removed from the federal calendar or replaced with Indigenous Peoples' Day, the essential point remains the same: Christopher Columbus's name and legacy should no longer carry the imprimatur of the United States government.

IV. The Moral Imperative

The abolition of Columbus Day is not a matter of political correctness or cultural erasure. It is a matter of historical integrity and moral responsibility. A nation that prides itself on its commitment to liberty and justice cannot, in good conscience, maintain a holiday that honors the man who initiated the centuries-long destruction of Indigenous civilizations in the Western Hemisphere.

The United States has acknowledged — through formal apologies, treaties, and policy — that its treatment of Indigenous peoples constituted a grave historical wrong. Maintaining a federal holiday in honor of the figure who set that catastrophe in motion is not merely tone-deaf; it is hypocritical. It sends a message that the nation's stated values of equality and human dignity apply selectively.

Conclusion

Christopher Columbus was not a hero who courageously bridged two worlds. He was a colonial administrator who enslaved, brutalized, and helped destroy the very people whose lands he claimed to have "discovered." The evidence for this is not ambiguous, contested, or newly discovered — it has been available for centuries, documented by Columbus himself and by those who witnessed his actions.

Abolishing Columbus Day as a federal holiday is a necessary step toward aligning our national commemorations with our deepest values. It is an opportunity to replace a false narrative with a truthful one, to honor the memory and resilience of Indigenous peoples, and to demonstrate that our democracy is capable of growth and moral reflection.

History does not ask us to forget. It asks us to remember — honestly. It is time to remember Christopher Columbus honestly, and to stop pretending that his legacy merits a place of honor on the national calendar.

Indigenous Peoples' Day (first proposed in 1977 at a UN conference and first adopted by a U.S. city—Berkeley, CA—in 1992) seeks to shift focus from Columbus to the histories, cultures, resilience, and contributions of Indigenous peoples. Its benefits include:

Introduction

For over a century, the United States has officially commemorated Christopher Columbus with a federal holiday, elevating him to the pantheon of American heroes alongside figures like Martin Luther King Jr. and George Washington. Yet beneath the elementary school rhymes of "In fourteen hundred ninety-two, Columbus sailed the ocean blue" lies a disturbing historical reality: Columbus's arrival initiated one of history's most devastating campaigns of colonization, exploitation, and genocide against Indigenous peoples. This essay argues that maintaining Columbus Day as a federal holiday represents an unconscionable celebration of conquest and cultural destruction rather than discovery and innovation. Columbus's Documented Atrocities

The historical record, including Columbus's own journals and the accounts of his contemporaries, reveals a man whose actions cannot be reconciled with modern celebrations of his character. Upon encountering the Taíno people in what is now the Bahamas, Columbus immediately assessed their value as servants, writing in his journal: "They would make fine servants... With fifty men we could subjugate them all and make them do whatever we want." This was not merely idle speculation—Columbus promptly enslaved local populations to mine gold, instituting quotas that, when unmet, resulted in punishments including amputation of hands.

Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish contemporary who initially participated in the colonization before becoming an advocate for Indigenous rights, documented the horrors that followed Columbus's arrival: "Endless testimonies... prove the mild and pacific temperament of the natives... But our work was to exasperate, ravage, kill, mangle and destroy." Under Columbus's governance in Hispaniola, the Taíno population plummeted from approximately 250,000-300,000 in 1492 to a few hundred by 1550—an annihilation driven by forced labor, disease, and direct violence.

Far from being merely a "man of his time," Columbus's cruelty shocked even his contemporaries. He and his men sexually enslaved girls as young as nine years old, and he permitted his men to violently "test the sharpness of their blades" on Indigenous bodies. Columbus's own letters document how he personally oversaw a slave trade of Indigenous people, writing: "Let us in the name of the Holy Trinity go on sending all the slaves that can be sold."

Glorifying Colonialism Through Celebration

When we celebrate Columbus Day, we implicitly commemorate and normalize the colonial worldview that Indigenous peoples were less than human—mere obstacles to be conquered in the pursuit of wealth and empire. The holiday's existence signals to Native Americans that the United States officially honors the man who initiated the genocide of their ancestors. This glorification perpetuates what historian Roxanne Dunbar-Ortiz calls "the myth of heroic and benign settlement in the formation of the United States."

Consider the psychological impact on Indigenous communities when government offices close and parades march to celebrate a man who wrote of his victims: "They are fit to be ruled." Celebrating Columbus communicates that colonial conquest and its accompanying dehumanization deserve commemoration rather than condemnation. This pattern repeated across the Americas. Columbus’s expeditions set precedents for the encomienda system, a form of slavery disguised as “missionary work,” and fueled the transatlantic slave trade. Historian David Stannard describes this period as the onset of the “American Holocaust,” with Indigenous populations reduced by 90% within centuries. Celebrating Columbus ignores this suffering and sanitizes a history of atrocity.

Myth vs. Reality: Dismantling the Hero Narrative
The myth of Columbus as a heroic explorer was popularized in the 19th century to foster national identity among European immigrants, particularly Italian-Americans. Yet this narrative erases Indigenous perspectives and historical truth. Columbus never set foot on what is now the U.S. mainland, and his voyages were motivated by greed, not curiosity.

Why Columbus Day Should Be Abolished as a Federal Holiday

Christopher Columbus Day, observed on the second Monday in October, is a federal holiday that celebrates a man whose arrival in the Americas in 1492 inaugurated an era of European colonialism marked by systematic violence, enslavement, disease-driven demographic collapse, and cultural erasure of Indigenous peoples. Far from a benign "discoverer," Columbus was a colonial administrator whose policies and practices directly contributed to the deaths of hundreds of thousands and set the template for centuries of exploitation. Retaining a national holiday in his name sanitizes history, marginalizes Native American perspectives, and signals that the United States continues to privilege the glorification of conquest over honest reckoning with its foundations. The Historical Record: Not Discovery, but Invasion and Atrocity

Columbus did not "discover" a virgin continent. The Americas were home to tens of millions of people with advanced civilizations, agricultural systems, legal traditions, and rich cultures long before 1492. What Columbus did was initiate sustained European contact that proved catastrophic for Indigenous societies.

Contemporary accounts from Columbus’s own journals and those of his contemporaries reveal a man obsessed with gold, slaves, and personal enrichment. In his 1492 diary, Columbus wrote of the Taíno people he encountered in the Caribbean: “They are so naive and so free with their possessions that no one who has not witnessed them would believe it. When you ask for something they have, they never say no. To the contrary, they offer to share with anyone.” He immediately interpreted this generosity as an opportunity for exploitation, noting they would make “good servants” and could be easily converted or subdued.

Within years of his arrival, Columbus instituted policies of forced labor and tribute. On Hispaniola, he established the encomienda system in all but name, requiring Indigenous people to deliver quotas of gold or cotton. Those who failed were punished with amputation, mutilation, or death. Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish priest who witnessed these events and later became an advocate for Indigenous rights, documented widespread atrocities: mass killings, the burning of villages, the hunting of people with dogs, and the routine rape of women and girls. While some revisionists dismiss Las Casas as exaggerated, multiple independent sources—including Columbus’s own writings, the testimony of other Spaniards, and archaeological evidence of population collapse—corroborate the scale of violence and disruption.

The demographic impact is staggering. Reliable estimates place the Indigenous population of the Caribbean at several million in 1492. By 1514, the Taíno population on Hispaniola had fallen to approximately 32,000. By 1542, Las Casas estimated only 200 remained. While introduced diseases such as smallpox played a major role, so did overwork, starvation, violence, and despair. Columbus’s governors continued and expanded these practices. The model of conquest, resource extraction, and forced labor established under his administration spread across the Americas, paving the way for further genocidal campaigns.

Columbus himself was eventually arrested and returned to Spain in chains in 1500 due to mismanagement and brutality under his rule. Even the Spanish Crown, hardly a progressive institution, found his governance unacceptable. Celebrating him as a visionary hero requires ignoring these primary sources.

The Symbolic and Cultural Harm of a Federal Holiday

Federal holidays carry significant meaning. They are days when government offices close, schools often hold programs, banks shut down, and the nation collectively pauses to reflect on values and history. By maintaining Columbus Day, the United States officially endorses a narrative that centers European conquest while erasing Indigenous suffering.

This is not merely symbolic. Many Native American communities experience Columbus Day as a day of mourning. For them, October 12 (or the federal holiday’s Monday observance) commemorates the beginning of genocide, land theft, and broken treaties. Cities and states that have replaced Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples’ Day—such as South Dakota (which has observed Native American Day since 1990), Minnesota, Wisconsin, and numerous municipalities including Denver, Seattle, and Portland—have recognized that a holiday should unite rather than wound. Continuing the federal observance forces taxpayers whose ancestors were victims of colonialism to subsidize their own marginalization.

The holiday also perpetuates myth over history. School curricula and parades that portray Columbus as a brave explorer who proved the world was round (a flat-earth belief he did not disprove; educated Europeans already knew the Earth was spherical) whitewash the violent realities of contact. This mythology served 19th-century nation-building during Italian-American immigration and the height of Manifest Destiny, but it has no place in a pluralistic 21st-century democracy that claims to value truth and inclusion.

Defenders of Columbus Day often raise several points. Some argue that we should not judge 15th-century figures by modern moral standards. This is selectively applied. We do not maintain federal holidays for other historical figures whose actions we now condemn, such as Confederate generals, despite similar “standards of their time” arguments. Moreover, even by the ethical standards of his era, Columbus faced criticism and removal from office. Contemporary Spaniards like Las Casas condemned the cruelty.

Others claim Columbus represents Italian-American heritage and pride. This is a legitimate cultural concern, but it does not require a federal holiday tied to a specific historical figure whose actions harmed other Americans. Italian-American contributions can be celebrated through existing holidays like Presidents’ Day (several Italian-Americans have been prominent in U.S. history) or through cultural festivals that do not double as national days of mourning for Indigenous people. Heritage should not come at the expense of historical accuracy or the dignity of other groups.

A further argument suggests abolishing the holiday erases history. The opposite is true. Abolishing Columbus Day as a celebratory federal holiday opens space for genuine historical education. Schools could use the date to teach the full complexity of 1492—European expansion, Indigenous civilizations, the Columbian Exchange (which included both devastating disease and important crops), and the long-term consequences of colonialism—without the distortion of hero worship. History is not erased by refusing to celebrate a flawed figure; it is distorted by insisting on hagiography.

Finally, some say the holiday is “not really about Columbus anymore” but about Italian-American achievement or simply a day off. If that is true, then the holiday has already become disconnected from its namesake, providing further reason to retire it and replace it with something more honest, such as a federal Indigenous Peoples’ Day that recognizes the original inhabitants of this land and their enduring contributions and resilience.

A Better Alternative

Abolishing Columbus Day does not leave a vacuum. Congress could establish a federal Indigenous Peoples’ Day that honors the more than 570 federally recognized tribes in the United States, acknowledges their sovereignty, and educates citizens about pre-Columbian history, the consequences of colonialism, and the ongoing struggles for treaty rights, environmental protection, and cultural preservation. This would align with the holiday’s original intent in some states and reflect a maturing national consciousness that values truth, reconciliation, and inclusion over outdated mythology.

Several countries in the Americas have already moved in this direction. In 2002, Venezuela replaced Columbus Day with Indigenous Resistance Day. Similar shifts have occurred across Latin America. The United States, which often positions itself as a global leader in human rights, should not lag behind in confronting its own colonial origins.

Conclusion

Christopher Columbus’s legacy is inextricably linked to colonialism, exploitation, and the immense suffering of Indigenous peoples. A federal holiday bearing his name requires Americans to collectively honor a figure who, by the standards of any humane ethic, bears responsibility for policies that led to death, enslavement, and cultural destruction on a massive scale. Maintaining this holiday perpetuates historical denial, disrespects Native Americans, and contradicts the values of an inclusive, truth-seeking society.

Abolishing Columbus Day is not an attack on Western civilization or an exercise in “cancel culture.” It is a necessary act of historical honesty and national self-reflection. The United States can acknowledge the full complexity of its past—including both the great achievements and the profound wrongs—without continuing to enshrine one of its most brutal initiators with official federal veneration.

The time has come to retire Columbus Day. In its place, let us create space for remembrance, education, and genuine respect for the peoples who have called this land home for millennia. Our national calendar should reflect who we aspire to be: a country that values truth over myth, justice over conquest, and inclusion over erasure. Abolishing Columbus Day is a small but meaningful step toward that more honest and equitable future.

Introduction

Every second Monday of October, the United States officially honors a man whose arrival in the Americas initiated one of the most devastating chapters in human history. The case against Columbus does not rest on applying modern sensibilities to a distant past; it rests on his own documented actions and the testimony of his contemporaries.

Columbus's own journals reveal his intentions from the moment of first contact. Upon meeting the Taíno people, he wrote: "They would make fine servants... With fifty men we could subjugate them all and make them do whatever we want." This was not idle speculation—it was a blueprint he systematically executed.

Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish priest who witnessed Columbus's regime, documented widespread torture, mass hangings, and the burning of villages. The Taíno population, estimated at several hundred thousand when Columbus arrived, was functionally extinct within fifty years.

Columbus also initiated the transatlantic slave trade, personally overseeing the capture and transport of Indigenous people to Spain. When enslaving locals proved insufficiently profitable, he proposed enslaving the Carib people entirely.

People weakened by overwork and malnutrition die from diseases they might otherwise survive.

Moreover, later Spanish policies demonstrated clear intent to destroy Indigenous populations when they resisted.
